analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating insured commercial banks from investment banking.
analysis.headline: A bill to re-separate commercial and investment banking drew 74 cosponsors from both parties but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the wall that stood from 1933 until 1999 between banks that hold insured deposits and firms that underwrite and trade securities. It would bar insured banks from being affiliated with brokers, dealers, investment advisers, or investment companies, bar securities-firm executives from sitting on bank boards at the same time, and force existing combinations to unwind within two years (extendable by up to one year) [S2] [S3]. It would repeal the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that created financial holding companies and financial subsidiaries, and it would lock in a strict Supreme Court reading of the banking-securities separation so regulators and courts could not narrow it [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers: the bill is designed to keep federally insured deposits from being used to back securities trading and underwriting, reducing the risk that speculative losses at a securities arm drag down a bank and trigger a taxpayer-backed rescue. Bank customers also gain from reduced conflicts of interest, since a bank could no longer push securities products through a affiliated in-house firm [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars insured depository institutions from affiliating with broker-dealers, investment advisers, or investment companies, keeping insured deposits and securities businesses apart [S2] [S3].

Prohibits officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving in leadership roles at insured banks, ending overlapping management of deposits and securities operations [S2] [S3].

Requires existing prohibited affiliations to be wound down within two years, with regulator extensions capped at one additional year and each exception reported to Congress with a detailed explanation [S2] [S3].

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that let financial holding companies combine banking with securities activities, and prohibits regulators or courts from interpreting the new separation more narrowly than the Supreme Court did in Investment Company Institute v. Camp [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large universal banks and their securities affiliates bear the cost: banks like those structured as financial holding companies would have to divest or unwind securities affiliates within two years, and securities-firm executives would have to leave bank boards. Some economists warn the disruption could reduce the convenience or lower the cost of one-stop financial services for customers.

drawbacks.text: Forcing banks to unwind securities affiliations within two years would be a major structural disruption; universal banks argue combining commercial and investment banking lets them serve large clients and absorb shocks with diversified income.

Critics of restoring Glass-Steagall note that the firms that failed or nearly failed in 2008 (such as Bear Stearns, Lehman Brothers, and AIG) were largely standalone securities firms or insurers, not the mixed banks Glass-Steagall covered, so the wall would not have prevented that crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real risk: it removes the structure in which deposits insured by taxpayers sit inside the same company as securities underwriting and trading. The cost falls on a handful of very large institutions rather than on most households, though the two-year unwind would be disruptive for the banks and their clients. The strongest counterargument is that it addresses the last crisis's structure rather than the risks (leverage, derivatives, and securities markets outside insured banks) that caused it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on January 14, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S5].
74 members cosponsored the bill: 70 Democrats and 4 Republicans [S4].
The only action ever taken on the bill was the referral to committee; no markup, hearing, or vote is recorded in its action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large universal banks came out ahead: they kept the ability to combine insured deposits with securities trading and underwriting, and the committee never had to hold a vote on ending it.

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the Glass-Steagall separation on January 14, 2015 [S1] [S3].

against.name: Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill during the two years it sat in his committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic (70 of 74 cosponsors were Democrats, with 4 Republicans), and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without a vote [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Large universal banks and financial holding companies
industries.note: The bill would repeal the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that allow these firms to combine insured deposits with securities underwriting and trading, forcing divestitures within two years [S2] [S3]. Their business model depends on that combination, whose costs in the event of failure fall partly on the deposit-insurance fund and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and investment companies affiliated with banks
industries.note: The bill bars insured banks from affiliating with these firms and ends overlapping bank-securities management, eliminating a channel through which securities firms reach bank customers and deposits [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Standalone community banks and traditional commercial banks
industries.note: Reinstating the separation limits competition from deposit-funded securities conglomerates and reduces the conflicts of interest that can steer bank customers toward in-house securities products [S2].
